beats.intro: Chapter two. [[sub]]Reported profit is only useful if the report is honest and the profit is repeatable. This chapter shows how an analyst tells good reporting from bad.
beats.quality: Two ideas, easy to confuse. [[frq]]Financial reporting quality asks: is the report relevant, complete, neutral and free from error? [[eq]]Earnings quality asks: are the results sustainable, and do they earn an adequate return? [[grid]]Put them together. High reporting quality lets you see the truth, good or bad. High reporting quality with low earnings quality shows a weak business honestly. And low reporting quality blocks the analysis, whatever the earnings really are. [[ex]]Toyota once reported a big jump in operating profit, mostly from a weaker yen. The reporting was clear, but that source of profit was less sustainable.
beats.spectrum: Reports sit on a spectrum. [[s1]]At the top: follows the accounting rules, is decision useful, and earnings are sustainable and earn an adequate return. [[s2]]Next: honest reporting, but the earnings may not be sustainable. [[s3]]Then, within the rules, but with biased choices. [[s4]]Then earnings management, through real actions such as timing a sale, or through accounting choices. [[s5]]Below that, reports that break the rules. [[s6]]And at the bottom, fictitious transactions. The lower you go, the less an analyst can rely on the numbers.
beats.shift: Biased choices move profit between periods. [[base]]Suppose true profit is one hundred in each of two years. [[agg]]Aggressive choices, like recognizing revenue early, lift year one to one hundred twenty, and leave year two with only eighty. [[cons]]Conservative choices do the reverse: eighty now, one hundred twenty later. [[tot]]The total is the same two hundred. Only the timing is distorted. That hides the true trend, and makes forecasting and valuation unreliable.
beats.triangle: Why would a manager report badly? Three conditions usually come together. It is called the fraud triangle. [[opp]]Opportunity: weak internal controls, a passive board, or standards that leave room for different choices. [[pres]]Pressure: to meet analyst forecasts, to earn a bonus, to protect a career, or to avoid breaking a debt covenant. [[rat]]And rationalization: the manager needs a story that makes the choice feel acceptable.
beats.discipline: What keeps reporting honest? Three mechanisms. [[reg]]Regulators, such as securities commissions, require filings and disclosure, including management's discussion of critical estimates. [[aud]]Auditors give an opinion on the statements. A clean, unqualified opinion is best. Qualified, adverse, or disclaimed opinions are warnings. But an audit gives reasonable assurance, not a guarantee. [[priv]]And private contracting: lenders, with covenants and their own checks, and buyers, with due diligence, have strong reasons to look closely.
beats.presentation: Management also chooses how to present results. [[rep]]Take reported net income of sixty. [[add]]Many companies publish a second, adjusted figure, also called pro forma, or non-GAAP. They add back restructuring of twenty five, and stock compensation of fifteen, and the headline becomes one hundred. [[flag]]Adjusting is not wrong by itself, and companies must reconcile the two figures. But if only negative items are excluded, and gains stay in, that is a hallmark of aggressive presentation.
beats.estimates: Even inside the rules, estimates move earnings. Take a machine that costs ten thousand. [[five]]Depreciate it over five years, and expense is two thousand a year. [[ten]]Assume ten years instead, and expense is one thousand. [[eps]]Profit is a thousand higher every year, with no change in cash. [[more]]The same lever sits in salvage value, the depreciation method, bad debt estimates, inventory cost flow, and whether a deferred tax asset can be realized. [[note]]Estimates are disclosed, so compare them with peers, and with the company's own history.
beats.cashflow: Cash flow from operations is harder to flatter, but not impossible. [[base]]Say operating cash flow is one hundred. [[stretch]]The company simply delays paying suppliers, and keeps thirty more. Operating cash flow looks like one hundred thirty. [[rev]]But next period the bill comes due, and the thirty reverses. [[class]]Classification is another lever. Moving an outflow from operating to investing makes operating cash flow look better. [[chk]]So compare operating cash flow with net income, over several years.
beats.signs: Finally, warning signs. Manipulation leaves tracks. [[rev]]Start with revenue. Here revenue grows ten percent a year, but receivables grow much faster. [[dso]]Receivables as a share of revenue climb. That can signal channel stuffing, early recognition, or even fictitious sales. Days sales outstanding rises. [[more]]Also check for inventory building faster than sales, costs that are capitalized rather than expensed, and net income that runs ahead of operating cash flow.
beats.wrap: Four things to keep. [[w1]]Reporting quality concerns the report. Earnings quality concerns the results. [[w2]]Aggressive choices lift today's profit by borrowing from tomorrow. [[w3]]Look for pressure, opportunity and rationalization, and weigh the discipline from auditors and regulators. [[w4]]Watch revenue, receivables, estimates, and cash flow against net income.
